name: Oil cleansing method
lead: The oil cleansing method is a facial cleansing practice in which a plant oil, or blend of oils, is massaged into dry skin to dissolve makeup, sunscreen and sebum, then emulsified with water and rinsed or wiped off.[1] Common blends pair a thicker oil such as castor oil with a lighter carrier oil, and it is frequently used as the first step of a double cleanse.[1]

Proponents say it removes oil-based debris without stripping the skin's natural lipids and can improve hydration and help manage acne.[1] Dermatologist guidance summarised in reference sources is cautious: it may suit dry or mature skin but may cause breakouts or irritation, especially in acne-prone or rosacea-prone skin.[1] Research on the method itself is limited.[1]

None found for the method itself

paras: Practitioners massage oil into dry skin, add warm water to emulsify it and rinse. Some recipes add a small amount of baby shampoo so the mixture rinses cleanly, and many people follow the oil step with a water-based cleanser.[1] Guidance in the source describes patch testing first and avoiding hot water and aggressive rubbing.[1]

Reference accounts trace plant-oil skin care to ancient Egypt, Ayurvedic oil massage and Edo-period Japan, where camellia oil was used. The modern version took shape in Western online forums in the mid-2000s and spread in the 2010s through Korean beauty double-cleansing routines, social media and commercial cleansing oils.[1]

Claims made for the method include removal of oil-based debris without stripping lipids, improved hydration, reduced dryness, acne management and mild anti-ageing effects.[1] Reference accounts say most cited support comes from studies of plant oils or emollients in general (for example on barrier function or on jojoba or argan oil for acne) rather than controlled trials of oil cleansing, and that some claims rest on small preliminary studies or testimonials.[1]

Reported concerns include pore-clogging with comedogenic oils such as coconut oil, allergic or contact reactions (especially to essential-oil additives), and irritation in people with rosacea, very sensitive skin or active infections. Oils can also feel heavy in humid climates.[1] The method is divisive among acne sufferers, with some reporting improvement and others breakouts.
No studies found. Related research on individual plant oils and emollients exists, but the oil cleansing method as a practice has not been tested in published trials.[1]

lore.intro: The method is debated in skincare communities, particularly for acne-prone skin, where reports of both clearer skin and breakouts circulate.[1]

claims.claim: Oil dissolves sebum and clogged pores better than foaming cleansers.
claims.believers: Proponents say like dissolves like, so oil removes sebum without stripping the skin.[1]
claims.experts: Dermatologist guidance cited in reference sources says it may suit dry skin but can cause breakouts in acne-prone skin; no controlled trial of the method exists.[1]

claims.believers: Some users report fewer breakouts after switching to oil cleansing.[1]
claims.experts: Support comes from studies of specific oils rather than the method; coconut oil and similar comedogenic oils are noted as potential pore-cloggers.[1]

card.summary: Massage oil in to dissolve sebum and makeup; popular and divisive for acne, with no trials of the method itself.
card.note: Comedogenic oils such as coconut oil may clog pores; irritation reported in acne- or rosacea-prone skin.

quick.overview:
The oil cleansing method uses a plant oil massaged into dry skin to dissolve makeup, sunscreen and sebum, followed by rinsing. It grew out of online forums in the mid-2000s and later merged with Korean double cleansing.

Supporters say it cleans without stripping skin. Dermatologist guidance is cautious for acne-prone skin, and the method itself is not well studied.
quick.mechanism: Oils dissolve oil-soluble substances such as sebum, sunscreen and makeup, and are then emulsified with water and rinsed away.
quick.risks: Comedogenic oils may cause breakouts, and additives such as essential oils can cause allergic or irritant reactions, especially in acne-prone or rosacea-prone skin.
